topic: creatives who feel AI flattens their distinctive personal style into a generic average even after feeding it references and examples
blind_spots: No quantitative data on how prevalent the flattening complaint is (no counts, surveys, or sample sizes) — most evidence is synthesis or anecdote.
Little first-person verbatim testimony from the affected creatives themselves; much of the strongest evidence is secondary synthesis (Sonar/report sources) rather than direct user voices.
No evidence on whether specific techniques (LoRA, voice profiles, fine-tuning) succeed for some users — only that improvements are 'partial,' with no breakdown of when/why steering works.
Music-specific firsthand pain is thin; the only direct music comment in evidence is dismissive of quality rather than about flattening of a personal style.
No vendor/model-specific attribution — evidence does not distinguish which tools or model versions flatten most.
Recency is unclear for the synthesis (Sonar) sources, which carry no dates, weakening confidence in how current these specific complaints are.
contradictions: Surface diversity vs. deep sameness: evidence states AI outputs can appear 'wildly different' in scene/subject yet are simultaneously described as homogenized and reverting to an average — the variety is real at the surface but contradicts the felt uniformity.

Productivity/originality gains vs. flattening harm: one source notes AI may 'enhance productivity and originality scores' while still making work more uniform and less valued, an internal tension between measured improvement and perceived loss.

Serendipity as benefit vs. liability: creatives reportedly appreciate surprising outputs yet simultaneously distrust them due to lack of control, a tension between valuing and fearing unpredictability.
